newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Digital CEO believes Intel to keep supplying chips.
newsitem.headline: Digital CEO believes Intel to keep supplying chips.

text.p: Digital Equipment Corp chairman and chief executive officer Robert Palmer said on Saturday he believes Intel Corp will continue to supply Digital with Pentium chips despite a legal dispute between the two computer giants.
"My guess is that they'll (Pentium) continue to service and sell to Digital," Palmer told reporters at the opening of a Singapore laboratory.
Palmer also said he was not softening his stand in the legal dispute, but added: "We're open to discussion about how things might be resolved."
The two companies are arguing over alleged patent infringement.

Industry executives have said they expect Digital to face increased commercial pressure as it moves ahead with the legal case, since like most of the industry, it has relied on Intel to supply processors for its personal computer products.
Intel has said separately it does not have an obligation to supply Digital with Pentium chips beyond the third quarter when Digital's purchase order runs out.
Palmer said comments about a possible cut-off have come from Intel's legal department, not its top executives.
He also said that given Intel's monopoly with Pentium, if a cut-off did take place, "we believe that the U.S. Justice Department would not fail to notice".
Palmer said that Digital itself was an important supplier to Intel and had no plans to stop its service and selling to Intel.
Palmer said Digital was well-positioned for growth after four years of investment.
"Digital feels very well-positioned at this time," he told reporters.
Despite management shake-ups, restructurings and layoffs, Digital, the fourth largest computer company in the United States, has lost billions of dollars over the past few years.
But the worst is over, Palmer said. "Most of Digital's restructuring is behind it, I'm happy to say. It's been a very difficult four years that we've been going through."
Digital had "made investments during the last four years for where we believe the market is going," he said.
He said the company was now well-placed in products in 64-bit computing, Windows NT, and the Internet, which should be key areas of growth in the information technology industry.
